explanations.explanation: Christ is the husband in Paul's picture. Paul says he promised them to one husband, “…to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.” Notice it's ONE husband, friend, not a lineup. I think Paul sounds like a man who takes a promise very seriously.

Paul is the one making the promise here, not the husband. He says, “…I promised you to one husband…” and then he names Christ as the One he's presenting them to. Paul is more like the guy carrying the ring pillow down the aisle. And the ring pillow guy never wants the spotlight, friend, he just wants nobody to drop anything.

Apollos, a Jew from Alexandria who was mighty in the Scriptures (Acts 18:24), is a real man, but he isn't in this verse. Paul's wedding picture has exactly one husband, and Paul names him: Christ. Paul says he promised the Corinthians to Him and wants to present them to Him. It's a short guest list, friend.

Eve it is. Paul says, “…just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning…” Back in the garden, when asked what she'd done, she said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.” (Genesis 3:13) Paul uses her story as a warning for the Corinthians, and I think that's a heavy thing to carry around.

Close, but Paul doesn't name Adam here. He says, “…just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning…” Adam is Eve's husband, and he's in the garden story too (Genesis 3:6). But in this verse Paul picks Eve to make his point about minds being led astray.

Abel, Adam and Eve's son (Genesis 4:2), comes along after the garden, so he isn't the one Paul reaches back to. Paul says, “…just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning…” The serpent talked with Eve in the garden (Genesis 3:1). Poor Abel wasn't even born yet, friend, he missed that whole conversation.

True. Paul says, “I am afraid, however…” and then names the danger: that their minds “…may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ.” He isn't telling them it's already happened. He's telling them what worries him, and a worry like that tells me he cares a lot.

This one is true, friend. Paul says, “I am afraid, however, that just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning, your minds may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ.” The word is “may,” so he's worried about what could happen. The devotion he wants for them is simple and pure, and I think that's a good thing to hope for.

explanations.answer: They put up with it very easily
explanations.explanation: That's what Paul says. If someone proclaims another Jesus, a different spirit or a different gospel, “…you put up with it very easily.” Notice he says easily, friend. I think that word is what worries him.

explanations.answer: They send the preacher away fast
explanations.explanation: If only, friend. Paul says the opposite: “…you put up with it very easily.” Nothing there says anyone gets sent away. He describes a church that puts up with it.

explanations.answer: They argue about it for days
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention any arguing. He says they “…put up with it very easily.” Easily is the word he picked, friend. I think a few days of arguing would have comforted him a little.

Right, he says he's “…in no way inferior…” to those super-apostles. That's from his own mouth in verse 5. Notice he's not saying he's better, just that he doesn't come up short. It's like being told you can't sit at the cool table, and you calmly say, “I'm fine right here.”

Paul doesn't see it that way at all. He says he's “…in no way inferior…” to those super-apostles. Far behind would be the opposite of what he says. He holds his head up here, and I think that's a good place to hold it.

That's a step further than Paul goes. He says he's “…in no way inferior…” which means he doesn't fall short. It doesn't mean he's greater in every way. Saying you don't fall short and saying you win are two different things, friend, and Paul says the first one.

Paul says the opposite about knowledge. First he admits, “Although I am not a polished speaker…” and then he adds, “…I am certainly not lacking in knowledge.” The speaking part is true, the knowledge part isn't. Hey, a rough speaker with real knowledge beats a smooth speaker with nothing to say.

That's right, it's false. Paul says, “Although I am not a polished speaker, I am certainly not lacking in knowledge.” He owns one thing and stands firm on the other. He even tells them, “We have made this clear to you in every way possible.”

explanations.answer: Preached the gospel free of charge
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul asks if it was a sin “…because I preached the gospel of God to you free of charge?” He calls that humbling himself so he could exalt them. Think about that question, friend. He's asking whether it was a sin to charge nothing.
The verse says nothing about leaders. Paul says he “…preached the gospel of God to you free of charge?” What he did was cost the Corinthians nothing.

explanations.answer: Refused to stay in anyone's home
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say a word about homes in this passage. What he says is that he “…preached the gospel of God to you free of charge?” That's the thing he did to humble himself. I'd love to hear the rest of the story, but I won't add to it.

Paul says it was someone else. When he was with them and in need, “…I was not a burden to anyone; for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my needs.” So the Corinthians weren't the ones covering him. That's the whole point of him not being a burden to them.

Yes, false. Paul says, “…the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my needs.” The Corinthians didn't carry that load, and Paul says he wasn't a burden to anyone there. Somebody else showed up when he needed it, and that's a good friend to have.

explanations.answer: He won't be a burden to them
explanations.explanation: Right. Paul says, “I have refrained from being a burden to you in any way, and I will continue to do so.” Notice the two halves: what he did, and what he will keep doing. He's making a promise here, friend, and he doesn't hedge it.

explanations.answer: He'll gladly accept it next time
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what he says. Paul tells them, “I have refrained from being a burden to you in any way, and I will continue to do so.” Continue means he's keeping at it. Next time looks the same as last time.

explanations.answer: He wants it sent to Macedonia
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. Macedonia comes up because brothers from there supplied his needs when he was in Corinth. What he tells the Corinthians is, “…I will continue to do so.” meaning not being a burden to them. Nothing in the passage asks for support to go anywhere.

True. Paul asks, “Why? Because I do not love you?” and then he answers right away: “God knows I do!” He calls on God as the One who knows his heart. He asks it and answers it in the same breath, friend.

This one is true, friend. Paul asks, “Because I do not love you?” and then he answers himself: “God knows I do!” He doesn't leave the question hanging for even a second. I think he wants them to be sure.

explanations.answer: To undercut men who want to seem his equals
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. He'll keep on, “…in order to undercut those who want an opportunity to be regarded as our equals in the things of which they boast.” So his free-of-charge preaching has a purpose. It's aimed at those men's opportunity to be regarded as equals.

explanations.answer: To win over the leaders in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say anything about Jerusalem here. His reason is given right in verse 12: “…to undercut those who want an opportunity to be regarded as our equals in the things of which they boast.” The Jerusalem leaders never come up in this stretch of the letter. I'd stick with what he actually says.

explanations.answer: To set an example for the Macedonians
explanations.explanation: Macedonia shows up in this passage, but not for that. The brothers from there supplied Paul's needs (verse 9). His stated reason is “…to undercut those who want an opportunity to be regarded as our equals in the things of which they boast.” So the Macedonians are the helpers here, not the students.
False it is. Paul says, “For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ.” That's a direct word from him. He doesn't dance around it, friend.

Age never comes up. Paul says, “For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ.” His problem with them is what they're claiming to be, not how old they are. Young or not, a fake is a fake.
Nothing in the passage says they're weary. Paul's word is “false”: “…false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ.” Tired has nothing to do with it.

That's it. Paul says, “…Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light.” He uses that to say it's no wonder when others put on a disguise too. Then he adds in verse 15 that it isn't surprising if his servants masquerade as servants of righteousness.

Pharaoh, the king of Egypt (Exodus 6:11), isn't who Paul names. His words are, “…Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light.” Paul is writing about disguises, and Pharaoh doesn't show up in this passage.

Jezebel, King Ahab's wife (1 Kings 16:31), is a name from the Old Testament, but Paul doesn't bring her up here. He says, “…Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light.” The one wearing the disguise is Satan, and Paul adds that it isn't surprising if his servants masquerade as servants of righteousness (verse 15).
Paul says the opposite. He ends with, “Their end will correspond to their actions.” That means what they do comes back around to them. Nobody slips away with it, friend.
That's right. Paul says, “Their end will correspond to their actions.” These men put on a disguise, but verse 15 says their end matches what they did. The costume doesn't change that.
